tldr: In unknown maze environments with cycles, we propose a distributed algorithm where agents avoid collisions and all reach an undisclosed goal using only 2-hop local communication and dynamic leader switching. We theoretically prove completeness and asymptotic convergence to an optimal full-knowledge strategy, and demonstrate its effectiveness and scalability in simulations with up to 625 agents.
overview:
There is a strong demand to safely and quickly guide large teams of robots to a destination in complex environments where maps are unavailable and communication is limited, such as in cave exploration or pipe network inspection. However, conventional methods are difficult to apply directly in scenarios where maps are unknown, global communication is impossible, and passages are narrow enough to cause collisions or make passing each other impossible.

To address this, the authors designed a mechanism where only a single lead agent executes a single-agent maze solver, while the other agents autonomously form a tree-structured following relationship (leader-follower relationship) tracking the agent immediately ahead. Even in mazes with cycles, by combining directed casts and local broadcasts to resolve follower path conflicts, and by passing the role to an existing peer (leader switching) whenever the lead agent is about to collide with it, they achieve collision-free navigation using strictly distributed local communication.

Through theoretical analysis, the authors prove that if the underlying single-agent solver is complete, all agents will reach the goal in finite time. They also prove that as the number of agents grows, the makespan (total completion time) asymptotically converges to that of an optimal full-knowledge strategy that knows the map in advance.

Simulations with up to 625 agents confirmed that the proposed approach safely reaches the goal without collisions. Compared to a naïve baseline where agents explore independently, it is dramatically faster and consumes less fuel, showing excellent scalability where the average travel cost per agent actually decreases as the swarm size increases.
contributions: Proposed a distributed Multi-Agent Maze Traversal (MAMT) algorithm that guides all agents to an undisclosed goal in general unknown graph environments containing cycles using only 2-hop local communication.
Theoretically proved that collisions are completely prevented by handing over the single-agent solver's exploration state via dynamic leader switching and maintaining an in-tree following structure.

Derived the algorithm's completeness, time complexity, and space complexity, proving that the makespan asymptotically matches that of an optimal full-knowledge strategy as the number of agents increases.
Demonstrated exploration efficiency and scalability far superior to an independent exploration baseline through simulations with large swarms of up to 625 agents across various grid maze sizes.

sections.heading: Tackling unknown mazes with local communication alone: The MAMT challenge
sections.summary: This section outlines the difficulties of multi-agent cooperative navigation in unknown maze-like environments like pipe networks and caves, and presents the paper's goals. By removing assumptions of global communication or known maps present in prior MAPF and exploration methods, it introduces a novel distributed algorithm for general graphs containing cycles.
sections.details:
Coordinating large teams of agents in unknown, maze-like environments is crucial for real-world infrastructure inspection and underground exploration. Prior research on graph exploration often assumed node-mounted beacons or global communication, failing to adequately address physical collisions or passing constraints between agents.

Meanwhile, Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF), actively studied in robotics, mostly assumes prior knowledge of the environment's map or relies on centralized computation. Although distributed extensions or unknown-environment variants exist, they are unsuitable for completely unknown environments where even the goal location is undisclosed.

Combining these challenges yields the problem of Multi-Agent Maze Traversal (MAMT). In MAMT, agents must incrementally uncover an unknown graph via local sensing and reach an undisclosed shared goal without collisions. Prior work either required global communication or was limited to tree-like structures (cycle-free graphs) when restricted to local communication, leaving general graphs with cycles unsolved with theoretical guarantees.

This paper extends the leader switching concept from earlier work to general cyclic graphs, proposing a novel MAMT algorithm with theoretical guarantees for collision avoidance and completeness using only local communication.

sections.heading: Problem setup: Narrow passages, local communication, and an undisclosed goal
sections.summary: The maze is mathematically modeled as an undirected graph, defining agent motion rules, collision definitions, and communication constraints. Total arrival time (makespan) and the average number of moved edges per agent (average sum-of-fuels) serve as evaluation metrics.
sections.details:
In this work, the environment is modeled as a connected undirected graph $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})$. The start node $s$ is a leaf node of degree 1, and an undisclosed goal node $g$ exists. Agents activate sequentially one by one from $s$; as soon as an agent leaves the start, the next agent becomes active.

Strict rules govern agent movement and collisions:
- In each time step, an agent either moves to an adjacent node or stays in place.
- Vertex collisions, where two or more agents occupy the same non-goal node simultaneously, are prohibited.
- Following collisions, where an agent enters a non-goal node at the same time step another agent leaves it, are also prohibited.

Communication and sensing constraints are very realistic:
- Agents know their own ID, whether their current or adjacent nodes are the goal, and whether adjacent nodes are occupied.
- Communication reaches up to 2 hops, and only along paths traversing unoccupied nodes (agents themselves act as communication obstacles).
- Agents use two communication primitives: directed casts sent toward a single specified edge, and local broadcasts sent across all adjacent edges.

The evaluation metrics are the makespan, representing the time when all agents reach the goal, and the average sum-of-fuels, which is the average number of edges traversed per agent.

sections.heading: Passing the torch: A cooperative algorithm powered by local communication
sections.summary: This section explains the autonomous coordination mechanism between the single lead agent (head) responsible for exploration and the followers tracking it. Through leader switching upon encountering obstacles and conflict resolution for vacant nodes (ResolveConflict), an orderly formation is maintained even in environments with cycles.
sections.details:
The core concept of the algorithm is simple. At any given time, exactly one agent acts as the "head," executing an arbitrary single-agent maze solver (such as DFS or BFS) at the front. All other agents follow another agent as their "leader," collectively forming an in-tree following structure rooted at the head.

To handle graphs with cycles, message types and procedures are meticulously designed:
- Status messages: Agents periodically broadcast their ID, goal arrival status, and current leader to their neighborhood.
- Conflict messages: Followers intending to move announce their participation in conflict resolution.
- Head messages: The current head announces the solver's internal state and who will assume the head role in the next step.
- Directed casts: Sent immediately after an agent moves toward the vacated node to notify the following agent of its previous location.

If the adjacent node chosen by the head is occupied by another agent, the head transfers the solver state and the head role to that agent, becoming its follower. This ensures that the exploration torch is smoothly passed even at dead ends or narrow spots where passing is impossible.

Followers run the `ResolveConflict` subroutine. When a leader moves two steps ahead and vacates a node, followers wishing to step into that vacant node perform deterministic arbitration. Only one winner advances; the losers designate the winner as their new leader and stay in place. With these local rules alone, agents prevent crowding and maintain viable communication distances.

sections.heading: Correctness and performance guarantees: Approaching the full-knowledge optimum
sections.summary: Using mathematical induction, the authors rigorously prove that exactly one head exists at all times, collisions never occur, and all agents reliably reach the goal. Furthermore, in the limit as the number of agents approaches infinity, the makespan asymptotically matches that of an optimal strategy with prior map knowledge.
sections.details:
The theoretical properties of this algorithm are solidly backed by the following lemmas and theorems:

- Head Uniqueness and Trajectory Equivalence (Lemma 1): At every time step, exactly one agent acts as the head, and it visits the exact same sequence of nodes as an isolated single-agent maze solver would.
- Collision-Free Execution (Lemma 3, Corollary 1): Entering unvisited nodes is done strictly by the head, and moves into vacant nodes are always limited to a single agent via arbitration; thus, neither vertex collisions nor following collisions ever occur.
- Maintenance of Leadership Tree (Lemma 5): The following relationships among all agents always form a directed in-tree rooted at the head, leaving no agent isolated.
- Goal Reaching in Finite Time (Theorem 3.1): If the standalone solver reaches a neighbor of the goal in $k_g - 1$ steps, all $n$ agents reach the goal within at most $k_g + 2(n - 1)$ steps.
- Asymptotic Equivalence to Full-Knowledge Strategy (Theorem 3.2): Let $M_{\text{FK}}(n)$ be the optimal makespan for omniscient agents possessing a complete map. The ratio $R(n) = M_{\text{Algo}}(n) / M_{\text{FK}}(n)$ with the proposed algorithm's makespan $M_{\text{Algo}}(n)$ monotonically decreases with $n$, satisfying $\lim_{n\to\infty} R(n) = 1$. Because the start is a leaf node, even an optimal strategy can dispatch at most one agent every two steps, allowing the exploration overhead to be completely amortized as the swarm size grows.

sections.heading: Computational complexity and memory: Practical overhead bounded by maximum graph degree
sections.summary: This section analyzes per-agent memory consumption and time complexity based on maximum graph degree $d$ and agent count $n$. Because communication is strictly local, each individual's computational load is capped at $d^2$ no matter how large the swarm grows.
sections.details:
Let $d$ denote the maximum degree of the graph. The complexity and memory requirements are as follows:

Space Complexity (Memory):
The maximum number of active agents within an agent's communication range simultaneously is $\min(n, d(d - 1))$. Maintaining neighbor lists and message information requires $\mathcal{O}(\min(n, d^2))$ memory. Since tracking the incoming neighbor for each peer takes up to $\mathcal{O}(d)$, the base algorithm's space complexity is $\mathcal{O}(d \min(n, d^2))$. Adding the single-agent solver's memory yields the total requirements (e.g., $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|)$ for BFS, or $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{E}|)$ for Trémaux's algorithm without marking the physical environment).

Time Complexity:
The computational cost of subroutine execution per time step is at most $\mathcal{O}(\min(n, d^2))$. The total number of steps depends on the choice of solver. Using Trémaux's algorithm, each edge is traversed at most twice, resulting in $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{E}| + n)$ steps and an overall time complexity of $\mathcal{O}((|\mathcal{E}| + n)\min(n, d^2))$. With BFS, backtracking occurs frequently, yielding $\mathcal{O}(((|\mathcal{V}|+|\mathcal{E}|)^2 + n)\min(n, d^2))$.

sections.heading: Large-scale simulations: Scalability validated with up to 625 agents
sections.summary: Simulation experiments were conducted using grid mazes with up to 625 agents. The proposed method succeeded without collisions across all trials, demonstrating that combining it with Trémaux's algorithm yields far superior efficiency compared to breadth-first search (BFS).
sections.details:
In evaluation experiments, grid maze sizes were varied across $l \times l$ ($l \in \{5, 15, 25, 35\}$) with agent counts $n \in \{1, 5, 25, 125, 625\}$, testing 20 random mazes per condition (with a timeout of $10^4$ steps). Three solvers were evaluated: Trémaux's algorithm, BFS, and random walk.

Experimental results showed that the proposed method (MAMT) using Trémaux or BFS achieved zero collisions across all trials, guiding every agent to the goal (random walk suffered timeouts in larger mazes).

Interestingly, Trémaux's algorithm, which progresses depth-first, demonstrated a substantially better makespan than BFS, which is typically intended to find shortest paths. For physical agents, the frequent backtracking movements characteristic of BFS introduce massive travel overhead.

Furthermore, when compared against a naïve baseline where all agents run solvers independently (yielding to lower IDs during collisions and swapping solver instances during cyclic deadlocks), the baseline suffered severe congestion as swarm sizes increased. In a $25 \times 25$ maze with 625 agents, the BFS baseline timed out in all 20 trials, and the Trémaux baseline timed out in 2 trials. In contrast, the proposed method finished every trial, showed lower average fuel consumption per agent as swarm size increased, and its makespan closely approached the optimal full-knowledge strategy.

captions.F3: Comparison of exploration behavior in grid mazes between Trémaux's algorithm (left two columns) and BFS (right two columns) at step counts $k=20$ and $k=100$. Dark gray indicates walls, and light gray indicates visited nodes. While BFS explores concentrically around the start point causing frequent backtracking, Trémaux's algorithm moves deeply along single corridors, minimizing physical travel loss.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: A summary of the study and future challenges toward real-world deployment. Having established theoretical guarantees and practical efficacy for local-communication MAMT in cyclic graphs, future work focuses on physical experiments and resilience against communication disruptions.
sections.details:
This paper presented a novel multi-agent maze traversal algorithm capable of traversing general graph environments containing cycles using only local communication. We proved that as long as the underlying single-agent solver is complete, all agents reach the undisclosed goal in finite time, achieving a makespan asymptotically equivalent to an omniscient shortest-path strategy as the swarm size grows large.

Simulations verified that the algorithm functions reliably even with large swarms of up to 625 agents, significantly outperforming independent baseline methods. Future work includes real-robot validation experiments and improving robustness against imperfect communication conditions such as packet drops and link outages.

takeaways: By dividing roles so that only a single lead agent explores while others follow in an in-tree structure, combined with dynamic leader switching, collision-free guidance is achieved in unknown cyclic environments using only local communication.

When the number of agents is sufficiently large, the overhead of exploring an unknown environment becomes negligible relative to total makespan, asymptotically matching the performance of an optimal full-knowledge strategy.

In graph exploration involving physical travel, depth-first style algorithms with minimal backtracking (such as Trémaux's algorithm) achieve vastly higher motion efficiency than concentrically expanding breadth-first search (BFS).

Even under a realistic local communication model where agents themselves block wireless signals, combining local broadcasts during leader handovers with directed casts to vacated nodes maintains unbroken following connectivity.
limitations: The approach assumes a synchronous, discrete-time model free of packet loss or communication delays; fault tolerance in real-world degraded wireless conditions remains unverified.

It relies on the structural constraint that the start node is a leaf node (degree 1) in the graph, meaning it cannot be applied directly to scenarios where multiple agents enter simultaneously from arbitrary interior nodes.
Physical experiments using real-world robots were not performed; evaluating how turning dynamics in continuous space and sensor noise affect cooperative behavior remains an open challenge.
